Accurate and real-time brain 
tumour detection and classification 
using optimized YOLOv5 
architecture
M. Saranya1 & R. Praveena2
The brain tumours originate in the brain or its surrounding structures, such as the pituitary and 
pineal glands, and can be benign or malignant. While benign tumours may grow into neighbouring 
tissues, metastatic tumours occur when cancer from other organs spreads to the brain. This is because 
identification and staging of such tumours are critical because basically all aspects involving a patient’s 
disease entail accurate diagnosis as well as the staging of the tumour. Image segmentation is incredibly 
valuable to medical imaging since it can make possible to simulate surgical operations, diseases 
diagnosis, anatomical and pathologic analysis. This study performs the prediction and classification of 
brain tumours present in MRI, a combined classification and localization framework model is proposed 
connecting Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN) and You Only Look Once version 5 (YOLOv5). 
The FCNN model is designed to classify images into four categories: benign – glial, adenomas and 
pituitary related, and meningeal. It utilizes a derivative of Root Mean Square Propagation (RMSProp)
optimization to boost the classification rate, based upon which the performance was evaluated with 
the standard measures that are precision, recall, F1 coefficient, specificity and accuracy. Subsequently, 
the YOLOv5 architectural design for more accurate detection of tumours is incorporated, with the 
subsequent use of FCNN for creation of the segmentation’s masks of the tumours. Thus, the analysis 
proves that the suggested approach has more accuracy than the existing system with 98.80% average 
accuracy in the identification and categorization of brain tumour. This integration of detection and 
segmentation models presents one of the most effective techniques for enhancing the diagnostic 
performance of the system to add value within the medical imaging field. On the basis of these 
findings, it becomes possible to conclude that the advancements in the deep learning structures 
could apparently improve the tumour diagnosis while contributing to the finetuning of the clinical 
management.
Keywords  Brain tumour detection, Brain tumour classification, YOLOv5 architecture, Fully convolutional 
neural network, MRI image segmentation, Tumour localization
The human brain is control over even some of the elementary functions and patterns of human conduct in 
society, including memory formation and recall, speech and language processing, cognitive functions such as 
thinking and problem-solving, and the coordination of limb movements and other physical activities1. Brain 
diseases often occur due to abnormal development or activity of brain cells, which can lead to structural damage 
and, in some cases, the development of brain cancer2. In 2018, a survey indicated a significant number of deaths 
worldwide were attributed to cancer, underscoring the profound impact of this disease on a global scale3. Within 
the realm of cancer, brain cancer stands out as particularly perilous due to its dangerous and rapid growth, 
ultimately leading to a high level of lethality4. To diagnose brain tumours, various medical imaging technologies 
are employed, each offering unique advantages in visualizing and assessing the physical components of the 
brain5. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is commonly regarded as the most frequently used and preferred 
medical imaging technique for diagnosing brain tumours among the various available methods6. Because of, MRI 
providing a superior visualization of contrast and spatial definition in comparison to other imaging modalities7.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) based techniques have grown popular in the identification of brain tumours in MRI 
images due to their ability to provide accurate and precise detection results8.
Recent breakthroughs in brain tumour detection have involved the deployment of a dual deep learning 
framework that integrates FCNN and the YOLOv5 framework for greatly improved diagnostic accuracy 
and real-time evalustion. This paper proposes NRMSProp, an optimized variant of RMSProp with Nesterov 
momentum for enhanced training stability and classification efficiency on imbalanced datasets. YOLOv5, 
chosen for its efficiency and object localization precision, surpassed U-Net and DeepLabV39inference speed 
and mAP, confirming its application potential in real-time medical environments. The model presented herein 
attained classification accuracy of 99.7%, F1-score of 99.8%, and detection speed of 48 FPS, facilitating effective 
tumour localization and segmentation. This model not only outperforms current models such as YOLOv7 
and VGG1910in accuracy and specificity but also minimizes labor, providing pragmatic usability in clinics and 
telemedicine. The incorporation of detection and segmentation, in addition to data augmentation and enhanced 
learning, is a significant leap in AI-assisted medical imaging.
The study focuses on AI implementation in detecting and categorizing brain tumours based on the MRI 
scans that play a significant role in studying brain conditions. Cerebral tumours remain the leading causes 
of death globally, and they can only be cured if diagnosed early. MRI has higher spatial resolution than the 
other imaging techniques; thus, it is the best modality for identifying such tumours. This work stresses that 
diagnostic methods should be enhanced so that the tumours at the initial stages can be detected easily because 
the high mortality rates affect those with brain cancer. Depending on the structures and diverse shapes of 
tumours, AI especially CNN, incorporates an important part in improving the diagnostic precision through 
automatically feature extraction and classification. However, the application of deep learning models always 
has some issues, for example, the requirement of large amounts of data, and the demand of rich computational 
resources, which limit the application in clinical practice to a certain extent11,12. To address these challenges, 
the proposed research presents a fresh method that integrates two elaborate deep learning frameworks, namely 
the Fully Convolutional Neural Network(FCNN)and You Only Look Once version 5 (YOLOv5), to form a two-
architecture around as a detection and classification technique for brain tumours13. This combines model not 
only identifies tumours but also enables segmentation masks to outline the tumourregion and boundaries, which 
will be beneficial for diagnosis and treatment planning. Extensions, including data augmentation and RMSProp 
with slight modifications, are also discussed within this regard further. Thus, the major novelty of this work is 
the proposed AI-based automated system with a high accuracy of brain tumours detection and segmentation 
and the possibility of using it in practice to enhancing and improving medical imaging techniques. The primary 
aids of the work are outlined as below.
•	 Merges YOLOv5 for real-time tumour detection with FCNN for accurate segmentation, improving accuracy 
in brain tumour diagnosis from MRI images.
•	 Introduces a Nesterov momentum-enhanced modified RMSProp optimizer to enhance training efficiency 
and stability for unbalanced medical datasets.
•	 Proposes a framework to categorize brain tumours into four types (normal, glioma, meningioma, pituitary) 
without excessive dependence on manual interpretation.
•	 Takes advantage of YOLOv5’s speed and efficiency for real-time tumour detection and is therefore ideal for 
clinical settings that demand rapid diagnosis.
•	 Utilizes data augmentation and streamlined architectures to enhance model performance on various MRI 
datasets and imaging scenarios.
Organization of research: The introduction emphasizes the clinical relevance of timely diagnosis, and the 
literature review that summarily reports deep learning methods. Methodology describes preprocessing of 
datasets, YOLOv5 adaptation, and optimization strategies. Results confirm enhanced detection speed and 
accuracy, verified on benchmarked datasets. The discussion contrasts the model with the latest techniques, 
highlighting its clinical relevance, whereas the conclusion summarizes future improvements for more extensive 
medical imaging applications.

Research gap
Brain tumour is one of the deadliest and hardest cancers, therefore early diagnosing is crucial in this illness. 
Even nowadays there are problems with accurate tumour localization and accurate classification of the tumour 
shape, size and location, despite the usage of modern techniques, for instance MRI. Automatic interpretations 
are as follows: Firstly, time consuming and have lower accuracy24, Second, most of them heavily depend on 
radiologists’ knowledge and experience, which is also not suitable for large-scale clinical applications17. Present 
methods for AI mostly have several restrictions, such as reliance on large annotated datasets, challenges in 
universality across different groups of patients, and computational issues in the implementation of AI in real-
time applications22. To fill these gaps, this research recommends a two-framework approach that involves the 
integration of YOLOv5 and Fully Convolutional Networks (FCCNs). YOLOv5 guarantees real-time and precise 
measurement of tumours, while FCCN offers precise boundaries between tumours. This system aims to increase 
diagnostic accuracy, decrease computational complexity, and build efficient and applicable solutions for early 
diagnosis and better treatment outcomes with the improved new NRMSProp algorithm and additional portions 
of data holdings.
Materials and methods
The proposed methodology highlights a new optimizer called NRMSProp, derived from RMSProp, to enhance 
the CNN performance for tumour classification from medical images. Through the integration of Nesterov 
momentum with RMSProp, NRMSProp improves the training speed, robustness and particularly the proportion 
ratio for the datasets that are unbalanced in term of the number of data points. This method incorporates 
momentum for the learning rate and makes an adaptation activity offering the model an expectation of the 
gradients to be leaned in future to moronize the weights. NRMSProp reduces the disadvantages of RMSProp 
where RMSProp completely fails to perform for big datasets and converges slowly. This algorithm calculates 
gradients gradually and incorporates them into the necessary corrections controlling for momentum and 
learning rates for weights. A similar process aids the model to converge faster and more stably, and is beneficial 
for classification application in tumour detection. The approach is most advantageous where medical image 
classification problems are concerned. YOLOv5 was chosen over U-Net, DeepLabV3, and Transformer-based 
models due to its superior real-time object detection capabilities, faster inference speed, and ease of deployment 
on edge devices. Unlike segmentation networks focused on pixel-wise classification, YOLOv5 excels in precise 
bounding box detection, which aligns with the study’s objective. An ablation study revealed that YOLOv5 
achieved higher mAP (91.2%) and faster FPS (48) compared to U-Net (85.4%, 12 FPS) and DeepLabV3 (87.1%, 
10 FPS), validating its selection. The proposed model was trained using a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 
0.001, selected through empirical tuning for optimal convergence speed and stability. NRMSProp optimizer was 
chosen for its adaptive learning and momentum properties, improving gradient updates. The training process 
involved 100 epochs with early stopping to prevent overfitting, using cross-entropy loss. Data was split into 80% 
training and 20% testing. These settings ensured balanced training, faster convergence, and high performance 
across accuracy, precision, and recall.

Dimensionality reduction
Dimensionality Reduction simplifies the dataset, and guaranteeing the removal of unhelpful information, but 
maintaining paramount features. This step helps in deciding what is computationally efficient because some 
terms in the model add excessive computational load.
Data augmentation
Augmentation is a method utilized to artificially boost the dataset by creating transformed versions of images 
within the training set. This is used to strengthen the generalization of deep learning models as well as suppress 
overfitting. In the study, augmentation techniques are most likely utilized to ensure the maximum diversity of 
the training dataset. Some of the typical image augmentation processes are:
•	 Rotation: Randomly rotating images within a certain range (e.g., ± 20°).
•	 Flipping: Horizontally or vertically “flipping” the images.
•	 Zooming: Zooming in or out of the image.
•	 Shearing: Applying affine transformations that slant the shape of the image.
•	 Brightness/Contrast Adjustment: Varying the “brightness” or contrast to simulate different “lighting con­
ditions”.
•	 Noise Injection: Adding Gaussian noise to simulate sensor irregularities.
•	 Cropping and Rescaling: Randomly cropping images and resizing them to the original input shape.
These techniques simulate real-world variations and help the model learn robust features.
Dataset partitioning: train/validation/test split
Partitioning of datasets is an essential technique in maintaining the validity of ML models. Splitting of the 
dataset in the research is done as follows:
•	 Training Set (usually 70–80%): Utilized to train the model. Only this set is generally applied augmentation 
to increase the training instances.
•	 Validation Set (typically 10–15%): Utilized during model training to optimize hyperparameters and avoid 
overfitting. It serves as a proxy to validate the ability of the model to generalize.
•	 Test Set (typically 10–15%): Applied at the end of the training process to measure the final performance of 
the approach. It gives an unbiased calculation of model accuracy.

YOLO V5 networks
To classify and detect the brain tumours using the YOLOv5 architecture shown in Fig. 3. YOLOv5 is a specific type 
of architecture used in deep learning models for object detection tasks. In this work, the YOLOv5 architecture is 
employed to identify tumours in brain MRI scans30.
In this approach, the FCCN model is first employed to classify different types of brain tumours, including 
non-tumour, glioma, pituitary, and meningioma, in medical images. The FCCN model is trained using a 
modified RMSProp optimization technique.After the tumours are identified using the YOLOv5 architecture, 
they are further processed using the FCCN architecture31. This processing helps in creating segmentation masks 
for the brain tumours, which improves the accuracy of tumour identification.The results show an impressive 
accuracy of 98.80% for tumour identification using the combined YOLOv5 and FCCN architectures.
The Fig. 3 illustrates YOLOv5’s architecture, featuring three components: CSPDarknet for backbone, 
Bottlenecks PP for feature extraction, PANET for the neck along with BottleNeckCSP concept unsampled Conv 
1 × 1 for more fused features and for the head Conv 1 × 1 during object detection. Sequential colours of the blocks 
enable identification of various aspects of the building architecture.
Backbone Network:
YOLOv5 employs a CSPDarknet53 backbone network as its means of extracting features. CSPDarknet53, an 
enhanced rendition of the Darknet framework employed in prior YOLO iterations, encompasses a multitude of 
convolutional layers and was meticulously crafted the features from the input samples.
Neck:
The network has a component called the “neck” that combines features from different sizes. It uses modules 
called PANet (Path Aggregation Network) and PANet-SPP (Spatial Pyramid Pooling) to make the features better. 
This helps YOLOv5 find objects of different sizes and scales.

Discussion
The proposed hybrid model combining Fully Convolutional Neural Networks (FCCN) and YOLOv5 architecture 
demonstrates exceptional performance in detecting and classifying brain tumours from MRI images34. To invent 
a method that would ensure simultaneously high accuracy of tumour detection and careful appearance analysis, 
the authors used YOLOv5 for accurate tumour position detection and FCCN to create segmentation masks35. 
Using this dual-model framework, the classification accuracy reaches 98.80%, which indicates the effectiveness 
of the present system in comparison with other systems developed for classification and localization. The 
model reduces the reliance on manual interpretation by automating tumour detection and segmentation that, 
in turn, eliminates unreliable diagnoses and improves efficiency36. The developed model is easily scalable 
for other modalities of medical imaging hence expanding its applications into other diagnostic fields. Also, 
the fact that the system is designed for real-time processing, currently it can be used in clinical environment 
due to time-sensitiveness of clinical decisions where precise results are required to be generated as quickly 
as possible during emergency37. Nonetheless, the model has some pitfalls. This is especially true for specific 
medical areas where it is difficult to obtain large well-annotated datasets, which it requires in order to perform 
well38. These considerations, such as greater computational complexity and requirement of high-performance 
computing components, limit the model’s applicability to settings that are resource-limited39. Moreover, the 
study questions applying the method on different MRI scanners and various patients’ populations still remain 
problematic, so further fine-tuning is needed for reliable results. This research lays a solid foundation for AI-
driven advancements in medical imaging. Future efforts should aim to incorporate multi-modal imaging data, 
develop 3D CNN architectures for improved segmentation, and enhance generalizability across diverse datasets. 
Addressing these limitations will amplify the clinical impact of such systems, paving the way for more accessible 
and precise diagnostic solutions. The study could be constrained by the dataset’s size and quality, which would 
affect model generalization. Pre-processing noise or inconsistencies in data can introduce bias, and the choice 
of thresholds can influence ROC performance. Overfitting is another issue, particularly with high-architecture 
models. Furthermore, the lack of testing in practical deployment constrains practical validation. Imbalanced 
classes can also produce errors, affecting the validity of performance metrics.
Conclusion and future work
The proposed research effectively combines Fully Convolutional Neural Networks (FCCN) with YOLOv5 
architecture to address the critical challenge of identification and differentiation between high- and low-grade 
brain tumours from MRI images. This enables the approach to attain almost perfect accuracy of 98.80% as well as 
the capability of providing the correct segmentation masks in clinical diagnosis. While providing a step-by-step 
approach of combining YOLOv5 for localization and FCCN for segmentation, the authors clarify its advantages 
aimed at increasing the diagnostic speed and improving the results. Through the use of the NRMSProp optimizer 
and better data augmentation strategies, the model shows good generalization and can easily be scaled up for 
more complex medical applications enhanced by Artificial Intelligence. This work avails the diagnosis process by 
cutting down the workload from radiologists and providing proper results to patients. The potential for growth of 
the benefits of this area in the future looks more than promising. By extending the set with utilizers of the robotic 
model from multiple modes of imaging data like CT and PET, the context to which diagnosis is made would be 
enriched, giving the model more depth. This or that, the use of 3D convolutional neural networks may enhance 
segmentation performance in different tumour sizes and shapes, providing more meaningful data for surgeries. 
Moreover, using cross-validation, different form of hyper parameter optimization such as grid search or even 
Bayesian optimization, can be applied to improve the model’s performance further. Proposed generalizability 
improvement should also address task-generating bias towards patients from certain demographic background, 
MRI scanners, or imaging protocols via domain adaptation. Lastly, the integration of explainability frameworks 
will help to improve the overall clinical uptake as well as promote the general acceptance of AI by clinicians, 
perhaps due to the fact that the decisions made using these applications will be transparent. Thus, responding to 
these directions, the system develops into a more extensive and invasive diagnostic platform.
